headline: The Only Trick to Being Good Is Doing Good
lede: Emmett Shear, the entrepreneur best known as a co-founder of Twitch, offered one of the more quietly devastating observations in recent social-media philosophy: that the bar for convincing him you're a good person is embarrassingly low. All you have to do is consistently show up and do things that benefit the people around you. He admits he falls for it every time.
body:
The joke, of course, is that there is no trick. The "deception" Shear describes is identical to the real thing. Consistent, voluntary effort on behalf of others in your life and community is not a performance of virtue — it *is* virtue, at least as Aristotle would have it. The Greek philosopher argued that character is not a fixed inner essence revealed by introspection but a pattern of habitual action. You become just by doing just things; courageous by acting courageously. The inner state and the outward habit converge over time.

Shear's framing inverts the usual anxiety. A great deal of modern self-help is preoccupied with *authenticity* — the fear that good deeds performed without the right inner motivation don't really count, that you might be performing goodness without possessing it. Shear treats that anxiety as misguided. If the behavior is consistent and genuinely directed at others' benefit, the metaphysical question of what's behind it stops mattering. The observer — and perhaps the actor — can't tell the difference, because there is none.

The word **consistently** does real work in the tweet. A single act of generosity is easy to perform and easy to dismiss as strategic. What's hard to fake across years, in the small and unglamorous moments of domestic and communal life, is showing up reliably when showing up costs something. That durability is precisely what convinces Shear — and what, he implies, should convince anyone. The con requires more sustained effort than simply being the thing you're pretending to be.

There is also a gentle rebuke in the post's lightness. By calling it a "trick" and confessing he "falls for it every time," Shear signals that he doesn't require grand gestures, elaborate credentials, or artfully professed values. He's watching what people do with their Tuesday afternoons. That's a more demanding standard than it first sounds, and a more democratic one: it asks nothing of background or eloquence, only labor directed outward.

concepts.definition: A tradition in moral philosophy, associated above all with Aristotle, that locates goodness not in following rules or maximizing outcomes but in the cultivation of stable character traits — virtues — through habitual practice. On this view, what you do repeatedly, especially when it costs you something, is what you are.

The philosophical puzzle of whether an action counts as morally good if the agent's inner motivation is impure, absent, or unknown. Critics of authenticity-obsessed ethics argue the question is unanswerable and mostly irrelevant: sustained prosocial behavior is its own evidence.
